---
title: "Lesson 1: Git vs. GitHub: what and why"
---

## Why version control?

Most of us have a folder that looks like this:

```
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_v2.R
analysis_final_v2_JL_edits.R
analysis_FINAL_actually_final.R
```

**Version control** replaces that with one file and a complete, labeled history of every change: who changed what, when, and why. You can go back to any earlier version at any time.

For public health work, this means:

- **Reproducibility.** You can show exactly which code produced a report.
- **Collaboration.** Several people can work on the same project without emailing files or overwriting each other.
- **Continuity.** When someone leaves, their work and its history stay with the team.
- **Safety.** Mistakes can be undone.

## Git vs. GitHub

| | **Git** | **GitHub** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Version control **software** | A **website** that hosts Git repositories |
| Where it runs | On your computer | In the cloud (github.com) |
| Needs internet? | No | Yes |
| What it does | Tracks changes to files in a folder | Stores a copy online, and adds collaboration tools: pull requests, issues, discussions, permissions, and websites (GitHub Pages) |
| Made by | Linus Torvalds (2005), open source | GitHub, Inc. (owned by Microsoft) |

An analogy: **Git is like Microsoft Word's "Track Changes," and GitHub is like SharePoint** where the tracked documents are stored and shared. You can use Git without GitHub, but GitHub needs Git.

Other sites that host Git repositories include GitLab and Bitbucket. The Git skills are the same everywhere.

## Three ways to use Git and GitHub

| Tool | Best for |
|---|---|
| **github.com** (web browser) | Quick edits, reviewing pull requests, settings, Discussions |
| **GitHub Desktop** (app) | Day-to-day work without typing commands. Recommended for beginners |
| **Command line** (Terminal / Git Bash) | Full control, automation, and working on servers |

RStudio and VS Code also have built-in Git panels. They do the same things as GitHub Desktop.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Repository (repo)** | A project folder tracked by Git, including its full history |
| **Commit** | A saved snapshot of your changes, with a message explaining them |
| **Local** | The copy on your computer |
| **Remote** | The copy on GitHub (usually called `origin`) |
| **Push** | Send your commits from local to remote |
| **Pull** | Bring new commits from remote to local |
| **Branch** | A separate line of work, so you can make changes without affecting the main version |
| **Pull request (PR)** | A request to merge one branch into another, with a place for review and discussion |

See the full [glossary](glossary.qmd).

## The big picture

```
 Your computer (local)                              GitHub (remote)
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
│ Working folder → Staging → Local repo │  push → │   Remote repo   │
│     (edit)        (add)    (commit)   │ ← pull  │   (origin)      │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘
```

1. **Edit** files as you normally would.
2. **Stage** (choose) the changes you want to save together.
3. **Commit** them with a message.
4. **Push** them to GitHub so others can see them.
5. **Pull** to get changes others have made.

Every lesson that follows builds on this loop.
